title: Life is about thinking
text:
I am grateful that David Shribman and Marshall Brooks spoke out loudly and clearly on the value of a liberal arts education (“A most precious possession,” Oct. 19 Weekly).
Although my major focus was modern history, my bachelor’s degree included wide-ranging courses such as French, mathematics, English, economics, creative writing, astronomy, chemistry, art history, and ornithology. But on graduation day, I didn’t realize that my liberal arts education had outlined my future. In the coming years, it became obvious that my direction, my life purpose, and my calling – although not enumerated on any Mercator projection or other map – were to think.
During the Vietnam War and my five years as a Marine officer and aviator, I wrote a weekly column for a military base newspaper, and then went on to a business career that started with an MBA and meandered into creative advertising, marketing, and consulting.
Early in my first advertising job in New York, I knew I needed more. I had to have a career that involved continuous thinking and a reliance on facts, cause-and-effect relationships, questioning “why,” and answering with practical and successful solutions.
Now, I am fourscore and more years old (that’s 80-plus), and I frequently ponder “To be, or not to be, that is the question.” I now know that thinking is my life.
Rod Carlson
White Plains, New York
